device.name: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition

workload.problem: damped harmonic oscillator x'' + 2 zeta omega x' + omega^2 x = 0, classical RK4, fixed step

arms.eagle_graph_steps: eagle graph, K fused steps per launch
arms.eagle_graph_steps_compact: eagle graph, K fused steps per launch + compaction
arms.eagle_graph_auto: eagle auto (eagle picks the launch mode)

arms.eagle_graph: The step written once as a hawk kernel; the whole loop runs on the device as one CUDA graph with a device-side stop guard, so a run is one launch with no host round trip per step. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 2.88 ms; spread S=1000: 25.5 ms; uniform S=1000: 28 ms. Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_compact: Adds an active-set map: the launch covers only the samples still running, rebuilt every 16 steps; it is made for batches that thin out (the spread configurations). On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 1.8 ms (0.625× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 13.1 ms (0.513× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 35.9 ms (1.28× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_reorder: Adds a physical reorder when the live samples spread thin over their warps, so the mapped reads stay contiguous; the final restore to sample order is inside its wall. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 2.26 ms (0.785× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 13.8 ms (0.541× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 37.6 ms (1.34× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_steps: The same step with one decorator argument, @hawk.kernel(steps=16): each launch runs that many steps per sample with the state kept in registers, as Warp's per-thread loop does, and the launches, guard checks and plane reads shrink by the same factor; its results are bit-identical to the eagle graph arm's in every cell. K is chosen by hand here; the eagle_graph_auto arm picks it at run time. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 2.69 ms (0.931× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 25.7 ms (1× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 28.4 ms (1.01× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_steps_compact: The K-steps kernel over the active-set map: the register-resident steps of the arm above, and the launches cover only the samples still running, so it fits batches that thin out. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 2.13 ms (0.738× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 8.48 ms (0.332× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 28.4 ms (1.01× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_auto: The same step with @hawk.kernel(steps="auto") on the active-set kind, and nothing to tune: it picks the steps per launch itself after every launch, on the device, so a batch whose samples all run to the end gets Warp-like fusion of up to 64 steps per launch, and a batch that thins out gets shorter launches with the active set compacted after each one; no sample takes more steps than the cap. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 841 µs (0.292× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 7.38 ms (0.289× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 27.6 ms (0.984× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 8 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_persist: The plain (not active-set) automatic kernel, forced through hawk's persist entry: one launch, no graph, no map, no policy kernel, no cap at 64 -- a grid of SMs blocks of 256 lanes each steal the next unfinished sample off a counter when their own finishes, so idle warps refill without ever rebuilding an index map; made for batches too large for one resident wave. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 1.36 ms (0.473× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 7.61 ms (0.298× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 27.6 ms (0.984× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_simulate: The same automatic kernel through eagle.simulate: the model, its state and its parameters by name, with no plan or plane binding to write; eagle deploys the kernel and builds the same device loop. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 847 µs (0.294× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 7.41 ms (0.29× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 27.6 ms (0.984× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 1 of 12 cells.
arms.eager_loop: The same kernels launched from Python one step at a time; the host sees the state after every step. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 4.93 ms (1.71× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 48.9 ms (1.92× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 52.2 ms (1.86× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.cupy_masked: NumPy-like array code on GPUs with no kernel to write; every sample is computed every step, so it fits dense batches where all samples run to the end (the uniform configuration). On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 30.5 ms (10.6× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 300 ms (11.7× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 296 ms (10.6× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_masked: The same array code in PyTorch tensors; it fits where the computation sits next to a PyTorch model or needs autograd. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 26.7 ms (9.25× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 265 ms (10.4× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 265 ms (9.46× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_graphed: The same PyTorch code with its launch overhead removed by hand: 16 steps captured as one CUDA graph and replayed, one host check per replay, the masking unchanged. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 23.4 ms (8.12× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 210 ms (8.24× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 209 ms (7.47× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_compiled: The PyTorch step under torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead"): Inductor-fused kernels replayed as a CUDA graph. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 7.33 ms (2.54× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 72.4 ms (2.83× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 71.6 ms (2.55× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.jax_vmap: The whole loop compiled once, a per-sample while loop batched with vmap; the same code runs on CPUs and GPUs and differentiates with jax.grad. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 8.12 ms (2.82× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 79.5 ms (3.11× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 79.5 ms (2.84× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.warp_kernel: Explicit per-thread kernels written in Python, maintained by NVIDIA and differentiable through wp.Tape; each thread runs its own sample and stops at its own step, so finished samples cost nothing. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 2.97 ms (1.03× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 28.9 ms (1.13× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 32.1 ms (1.15× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.cpu_openmp: The same hawk kernel on the host through eagle's OpenMP team, for machines without a GPU. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 3.73 ms (1.29× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 31.2 ms (1.22× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 43.2 ms (1.54× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 3 of 12 cells.
